justification:
Full technical pass plus the five specific items requested, including independent reproduction of the article's central benchmark.

RUN-CODE: PASS, blocks=15 executed=7, no failures/warnings.

ITEM 1 (central claim -- array beats trie on memory AND time at every size, no crossover through 200,000): This is real and reproducible, not an artifact. I extracted all three benchmark code blocks (trie-memory-small, trie-extreme-sharing, trie-vs-array-benchmark) verbatim and ran them independently two ways: (a) as a Release-configuration csproj, which gave different absolute numbers due to JIT/tiering differences, and (b) via `dotnet run <file>.cs` -- a file-based program, the exact mechanism `tools/run-code.mjs` itself uses (`spawnSync('dotnet', ['run', srcFile, ...])`). Method (b) reproduced the article's memory numbers byte-for-byte across three separate runs: 50/500/5,000-word table (0.5/69.8, 4.0/604.6, 39.1/5324.1 KB, ratios 146.4x/151.5x/136.0x) and the extreme-sharing table (11.8 KB array / 81.3 KB trie) matched exactly. The four-size benchmark's memory column (array/trie MB: 0.00/0.59, 0.04/5.19, 0.38/43.19, 1.53/158.00) also matched exactly across repeated runs -- these GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread deltas are deterministic given the fixed RNG seeds and are not cherry-picked. The timing columns showed normal run-to-run jitter (as expected and as the article's 'one run on this machine' framing already accounts for, with the output block itself wildcarded), but the qualitative pattern -- array faster at every size, gap not closing through n=200,000 -- reproduced consistently across every run I performed. On the methodology question: counting matches via `CountWithPrefix`/`CountWithPrefixSorted` rather than materializing them is sound and, if anything, conservative in the trie's favor -- a real prefix-search API would need the trie to concatenate `prefix + suffix` per match (as the earlier `StartsWith` demo does) while the array already holds intact string references, so counting removes an allocation cost that would otherwise make the trie look worse, not better. The explanatory mechanism the article gives (a `Dictionary<char,TrieNode>` lookup chases a pointer to a separately heap-allocated node, vs. `string.CompareOrdinal` running as a tight comparison over contiguous memory) is accurate: I fetched dotnet/runtime's `String.Comparison.cs` and confirmed `CompareOrdinal` delegates to `SpanHelpers.SequenceCompareTo`, which is genuinely vectorized (SIMD) for a comparison over contiguous memory, and comments in that source explicitly discuss 8-byte alignment for 'better perf... and SIMD'. So the claimed mechanism is real, not invented, though it is not cited inline (see minor issue below).

ITEM 2 (Morrison/PATRICIA restraint): Confirmed by full-text search of the article -- 'Morrison', 'PATRICIA' (in that spelling), and '1968' each appear exactly once, all in the single clause 'A radix tree (also called a compressed trie, or historically a Patricia trie)'. No sentence asserts who introduced the term, when, or in what paper; Morrison's name is never used. This is the restraint the round brief asked me to verify, and it holds -- the article does not assert anything about the 1968 paper it could not verify.

ITEM 3 (memory-ratio direction, ~150x at low sharing vs ~7x at heavy sharing): The direction is correct and I independently confirmed the actual numbers (see item 1). The mechanism holds up under a structural count: for the extreme-sharing case (676 words, 20 chars, 18-char shared prefix), the trie has an 18-node shared spine + up to 26 first-branch nodes + 676 leaf/word nodes -- roughly ~720 TrieNode objects for 676 words (~1.07 nodes/word), because nearly all of the length is stored once. For the ~random low-sharing case, the trie has close to one node per character actually inserted (little sharing beyond the first 1-2 levels for a 26-letter alphabet), i.e. roughly 7 nodes/word for average word length ~7 -- about 7x the nodes-per-word of the shared case, which is the right order of magnitude to explain a ~150x -> ~7x swing relative to an array whose own cost (references to already-existing strings) barely depends on sharing at all. Sound and correctly explained in the article's own prose ('most of the trie's cost is per-node bookkeeping... not per-character storage, while the array's cost is close to zero marginal bytes per word').

ITEM 4 (compressed trie / radix tree explanation and the fib_trie citation): The definition given (a node with exactly one child and not itself a stored word gets merged into the edge above it, so a chain becomes one edge carrying a substring) is the standard radix-tree/PATRICIA construction and matches Sedgewick & Wayne's and general textbook treatments of R-way tries with one-way branching removed. The fib_trie citation is used correctly: the kernel doc explicitly describes skipping runs of bits that 'represent a single path with no deviations' in the real IPv4 forwarding-table implementation, which does support the 'not hypothetical... production tries are actually built when memory matters' claim. The article is honest that it gives no implementation and that Insert would need to split edges -- a real, uncited-but-uncontroversial fact about radix-tree insertion.

ITEM 5 (Trie.Remove correctness): Traced the recursive removal by hand against the article's own three-step removal script and reproduced its exact printed output. `Remove("car")` clears the `r` node's `IsWord` but does not prune, because `r` still has a child (`e`, on the path to `care`) -- correct, `Contains("car")=False, Contains("care")=True` follows. `Remove("dot")` clears `t`'s flag and, since `t` is childless, unlinks it from `o`; `o.IsWord` is still true ("do" not yet removed) so no further pruning happens at that level -- correct. `Remove("do")` then clears `o`'s flag; `o` is now both non-word and childless, so it unlinks from `d`; `d` was never itself a word and is now childless too, so it unlinks from the root -- leaving no trace of either word, matching `StartsWith("do") = []`. The pruning guard (`removed && !child.IsWord && (child.Children is null || child.Children.Count == 0)`) is evaluated only after the recursive call returns, correctly implementing bottom-up pruning, and `node.Children` is provably non-null at the point it calls `.Remove(c)` (it was already dereferenced two lines earlier in the same stack frame). The implementation is correct, including the no-op case (removing a word not present returns `false` without mutating anything). This is real, correct code, not hand-waved pseudocode.

OTHER FINDING (why the score is capped): The article's own diagrams contain an internally inconsistent node count. Figure 2's `<desc>` states 'Five nodes in total, down from eleven.' Counting the actual SVG elements: Figure 1 has exactly 11 `<circle>` elements (1 small root marker + 10 boxed character nodes: c,a,r,e,f,u,l,d,o,t), so 'eleven' is only correct if the root marker is counted as one of the nodes. Figure 2 has exactly 6 `<circle>` elements (the same small root marker + 5 boxed nodes: car,care,careful,do,dot), so 'five' is only correct if the root marker is NOT counted. These two counts use opposite conventions for the same kind of element (the root marker, drawn identically in both figures), so the comparison 'five... down from eleven' cannot be right under any single consistent rule -- it is either 'six... down from eleven' (root counted both times, matching the true number of TrieNode objects that would actually be allocated, including the mandatory root) or 'five... down from ten' (root excluded both times). This is a concrete, checkable claim in reader- and screen-reader-facing content (the accessible `<desc>`) that does not hold up, which is exactly the kind of thing this round's technical pass is meant to catch. Per the brief's rule that a single factual error caps the score at 7, I am capping here despite the rest of the article -- code, citations, and the central empirical claim -- being unusually well verified.

No fabricated numbers, no misattributed citations, no code that fails to run, no unscoped only/always/never claims found elsewhere. All complexity claims are stated with the operation and case they apply to (trie insert/contains/prefix-walk O(L); binary search O(log n) to find the start, O(m) to scan matches; adjacency to the BST article's degenerate-tree caveat is correctly distinguished from the trie's arrival-order independence).
